title: What's this, where's that
goal: Point at things and ask about them — while swallowing one word-order surprise: Egyptian demonstratives stand AFTER the noun, not before it.
bekal: point at things with ده، دي، دول and put them in the right place
use الـ and pronounce it according to the letter that follows
say there is and there isn't with فيه and مافيش

dialogs.title: حوار — في أوضة بودي الجديدة
dialogs.intro: Budi has just moved into a rented room in Dokki. The landlady, Umm Sayed, shows him around.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: اتفضل يا بني. دي الأوضة بتاعتك.
lines.baca: itfaḍḍal ya ibni. di l-ōḍa bitaa‘tak.
lines.id: Come in, son. This is your room.
lines.literal: please O my-son. this the-room of-yours.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Wow! This room is really big.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: Yes, and it has a balcony too.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.baca: da s-sakhkhaan. wi d-dulaab da lihduumak.
lines.id: That's the water heater. And this wardrobe is for your clothes.
lines.literal: this the-heater. and the-wardrobe this for-your-clothes.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Is there internet in the house?

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: أيوه، فيه. بس مافيش تكييف، معلش.
lines.baca: aywa, fiih. bas mafiish takyiif, ma‘lesh.
lines.id: Yes, there is. But there's no air conditioning, sorry.
lines.literal: yes, there-is. but there-isn't cooling, never-mind.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: No problem. And where's the kitchen?

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.id: The kitchen is over there, next to the bathroom.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: دي كتب ابني. هو في السفر دلوقتي.
lines.baca: di kutub ibni. huwwa fis-safar dilwa’ti.
lines.id: Those are my son's books. He's traveling right now.
lines.literal: these books my-son. he in the-travel now.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Okay. And does this window face the street?
lines.literal: okay. and the-window this on the-street?

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: لأ، على الحديقة. الشارع من الناحية التانية.
lines.id: No, the garden. The street is on the other side.
lines.literal: no, on the-garden. the-street from the-side the-second.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Better that way. Thank you, Hagga.

lines.speaker: أم سيد:
lines.text: العفو. أي حاجة، أنا في الدور التاني.
lines.baca: il-‘afw. ayyi haaga, ana fid-dōr it-taani.
lines.id: You're welcome. If you need anything, I'm on the second floor.
lines.literal: pardon. any thing, I in the-floor the-second.

notes: **Demonstratives stand AFTER the noun.** الأوضة دي is literally "the room this", in the order "room-this". Fusha puts it in front (هَذِهِ الْغُرْفَةُ); Egyptian puts it behind. It feels backwards at first, but it's one fixed rule — and it never changes.

**But ده can also stand in front, and then the meaning changes.** ده كتاب means "this is a book" — a complete sentence. Whereas الكتاب ده means "this book" — just a phrase, not yet a sentence. The whole difference lies in الـ.

**The word فيه means "there is", and it never changes form.** فيه إنترنت (there's internet), فيه ناس (there are people), فيه مشكلة (there's a problem). The negative is one word: مافيش *mafiish*, which is also a complete sentence on its own when someone asks whether something is there.

**Don't mix up فيه "there is" and فيه "in it".** The second appears in line three of the dialogue: وفيها بلكونة — "and in it there's a balcony", with the ending ـها pointing back to the room. Context always tells them apart.

**The word حاجة means "something" or "thing", not "need".** It's one of the most frequent words in Egyptian: أي حاجة (anything), مافيش حاجة (nothing), عايز حاجة؟ (want something?). It happens to sound like the title for a woman who has made the pilgrimage, and the dialogue above uses both.

**The address يا حاجة is used for a respected older woman**, whether or not she has actually made the pilgrimage to Mecca. The masculine form is يا حاج. Using it with an older person whose name you don't know is the safest and most polite option in Egypt.

grammars.title: Three demonstratives (ده، دي، دول) and where they go
body: Egyptian has just three demonstratives for "this", and all three are also used for "that". Distance isn't marked; if it needs stressing, people add هناك.
after: Look at the third row: plural objects are treated as **feminine singular** in Egyptian. So "these books" isn't الكتب دول but الكتب دي, and the adjective goes feminine too: الكتب دي حلوة.
The word دول is only used for plural **people**: الطلبة دول (these students), الولاد دول (these kids). This rule feels strange at first and becomes instinct after a few weeks.
To stress distance, add هناك after it: الراجل ده هناك (that man over there). Egyptian has no separate word for "that" the way English does.

grammars.title: The prefix الـ and the letters that absorb it
body: If you've learned to read the Qur'an or studied Fusha, you already know this. The prefix الـ is always written the same, but it's pronounced two ways depending on the letter after it.
after: The rule is the same as in Fusha: sun letters swallow the l sound, moon letters don't. The only thing to watch is that Egyptian pronounces the prefix as **il-**, not **al-**.
The last row is an Egyptian extra that doesn't exist in Fusha: because ج is pronounced **g** here, it swallows the l sound like a sun letter. So الجامعة sounds like *ig-gam‘a*, not *il-gam‘a*.

sections.title: Around the house and in your bag

blocks.text: Some of these may ring a bell: ترابيزة and بلكونة came from Italian through the port of Alexandria, and the second is the same word as English *balcony*. If you know some Fusha, كتاب، كرسي، مفتاح، باب need no introduction either.

blocks.title: The word فلوس is always plural
items: The word فلوس *fuluus* means money, and it's always plural — there's no singular in everyday use. Adjectives that go with it are plural too: الفلوس دي كتير.
It comes from فلس, an ancient copper coin, and the same root gives مفلس *muflis* — "broke, bankrupt".
To ask how much something costs, the phrase is بكام؟ *bikaam?* — and that's covered in full in unit 5.

blocks.text: One word, فيه, covers everything English says with "there is / there are", and the negative is one word too. No changes of form at all.

blocks.text: The phrase مافيش مشكلة is one of the ones you'll hear most in Egypt, and its meaning is much wider than its translation. It's used to reassure, to accept an apology, to say that everything's fine — and sometimes to close a matter that isn't actually fine at all.

items: Is there internet in this house?

exercises.prompt: Fill in ده، دي or دول.
Answer with فيه or مافيش to match the situation.
items: You're asked whether there's a problem, and there isn't.
You're asked whether there's food in the kitchen, and there is.
You're asked whether there's anyone in the room, and there's nobody.
You're asked whether there's hot water, and there is.
You're asked whether there's time now, and there isn't.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

مافيش مشكلة. — أيوه، فيه أكل في المطبخ. — لأ، مافيش حد في الأوضة. — أيوه، فيه مية سخنة. — لأ، مافيش وقت دلوقتي.
